summary:
San Luis stands under the national framework: Argentina's Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012 after passing the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and the Senate 55 votes to one abstention, allows a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval, and an 'X' marker has been available on the national identity document since 2021. The United Nations described the statute as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region, and Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010.

For a visitor the operating position has narrowed without the statute being repealed. On 5 February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei published decree DNU 62/2025 amending Article 11 of the Gender Identity Law to bar under-18s from gender-affirming surgical and hormonal interventions, alongside decree DNU 61/2025 altering prison-sentencing law to change the placement of trans detainees. Both decrees apply nationally, to every province, including San Luis. Legal experts and LGBT+ organisations interviewed by Agencia Presentes called the measures unconstitutional, argued that abruptly suspending adolescent treatments endangers trans youth, and signalled a judicial challenge.

Activists from organisations named for Diana Sacayán and Lohana Berkins told the Washington Blade in April 2025 that the community faces a chaotic and desperate situation, and that the 2012 Gender Identity Law, while still formally in force, is no longer guaranteed in practice.
tangentialFactors:
Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented peak in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity over the year, a rate of roughly one every 38 hours, with trans women bearing a disproportionate share of the harm, according to Agencia Presentes.

The judicial response to gender-motivated killing is contested. In April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of the trans activist Diana Sacayán while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance removed by an appeals court in 2020, so that aggravation is not currently applied in that line of cases.

Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records negative assessments for same-sex relations, gender recognition and the registration of civil-society organisations, and marks a deterioration against the earlier statutory position.
localsOnly:
Residents of San Luis are affected by the elimination of the national Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry under President Milei and by the dismissal of trans hires made under the federal Trans Labor Quota Law, which reserves one per cent of public-sector posts; activists told the Washington Blade that the quota is no longer being implemented.

DNU 61/2025 changes how trans detainees are housed under Argentina's prison-sentencing law, a measure that governs provincial prison systems including San Luis. Legal experts and LGBT+ organisations described both February 2025 decrees as unconstitutional, and the decrees face judicial challenge, so the enforceable position for residents may be revised by the courts.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether San Luis province has issued its own implementing instructions on trans detainee placement under DNU 61/2025 is not sourced here, and the inventory records no San Luis-specific enforcement data on the Gender Identity Law, no provincial anti-discrimination statute named for this jurisdiction, and no recorded hate-crime figures broken down by province.

The Washington Blade's account of the Trans Labor Quota Law being abandoned rests on activist statements rather than on an official repeal; the inventory does not confirm whether the quota statute remains formally on the books.

The outcome of the judicial challenge to DNU 62/2025 and DNU 61/2025 is unresolved in the sources provided, as is whether courts will restore the travesticidio aggravating circumstance in gender-motivated killings.
